precepts.text: In the dearth the people mortgaged lands and borrowed for the king's tribute, and brought their sons and daughters into bondage; that is how brethren came into servitude.
precepts.point: Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
Nehemiah 5 shows how brethren came into servitude in the first place: “And there was a great cry of the people and of their wives against their brethren the Jews.” Some said, “We have mortgaged our lands, vineyards, and houses, that we might buy corn, because of the dearth.” Others said, “We have borrowed money for the king’s tribute, and that upon our lands and vineyards.”

And some had gone further: “we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters are brought unto bondage already: neither is it in our power to redeem them; for other men have our lands and vineyards.” That is the Hebrew servant of Exodus 21: a brother sold into service in the dearth, for corn or for the king’s tribute, or a son or daughter brought into bondage by a father who could not redeem them.

note.label: CHRIST THE GOD THE REDEEMER

precepts.why:
“And I said unto them, We after our ability have redeemed our brethren the Jews, which were sold unto the heathen”. The same word that is translated buy in Deuteronomy 28:68 is used here by Nehemiah, and here it is translated redeemed. Nehemiah and them went and paid money and bought back their brothers that were sold to the heathens. They redeemed them; they paid money and got them back.

So in Deuteronomy 28:68, when we are sold unto our enemies “and no man shall buy you”, it means nobody would be able to purchase us back or redeem us. You can’t fool us; we understand the Bible.

Nehemiah keeps on: “and will ye even sell your brethren? or shall they be sold unto us? Then held they their peace”.

note.label: Sons of Jacob: A Shadow of Things to Come

precepts.why: “From the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah” … “that is, twelve years.” For 12 years Nehemiah was the governor of Israel, ruling over us and teaching us God’s laws.

moments.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free
THE BLACK BOULÉ & BOURGEOISIE IN THE BIBLE

points: After the return from Persia, the poor mortgaged their lands and sold their children to their own brethren.
Nehemiah set a great assembly against the nobles, and they restored the lands and required nothing.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

points: There is a great cry of the people and their wives against their brethren the Jews.
Even in the middle of the outside threat, a wrong rises up inside the camp among the people themselves.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Some say their sons and daughters are many, and they take up corn for them that they may eat and live.
The people are burdened, having to trade for grain simply to keep their large households alive.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Others say they have mortgaged their lands, vineyards, and houses to buy corn because of the dearth.
The famine forces the people to put up their property just to feed their families.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Still others say they have borrowed money for the king's tribute upon their lands and vineyards.
The heavy tax drives the people into debt against the very land they depend on.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Their flesh is as the flesh of their brethren, yet they are bringing their sons and daughters into bondage, and some daughters are already brought to bondage with no power to redeem them.
Their own brethren are enslaving them over debt though they are one flesh, one people just come out of captivity.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: When Nehemiah hears their cry and these words he is very angry.
The oppression of the people by their own brethren stirs his anger.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Nehemiah consults with himself, rebukes the nobles and rulers for exacting usury each from his brother, and sets a great assembly against them.
He brings a great multitude before the nobles to make the point plain that lending against their brethren for gain is usury and wrong.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Nehemiah reminds them that he and his have redeemed their brethren the Jews from the heathen, and asks if they will now sell their own brethren, so that they hold their peace and find nothing to answer.
The nobles are silenced because they have no answer for enslaving the same brothers others labored to buy back from the heathen.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Nehemiah says it is not good what they do, and asks if they ought not to walk in the fear of God because of the reproach of the heathen their enemies.
Their conduct toward their brethren should be governed by the fear of the Most High, especially with the enemies watching.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Nehemiah says he, his brethren, and his servants might also exact money and corn, but pleads that they leave off this usury.
Even those with the right to lend are called to give up usury against their own people.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Nehemiah asks them to restore that same day the lands, vineyards, oliveyards, and houses, and the hundredth part of the money, corn, wine, and oil they had exacted.
He calls for full and immediate restoration of what was taken from the brethren.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: They agree to restore everything and require nothing, so Nehemiah calls the priests and takes an oath of them to do according to this promise.
The promise is bound by oath before the priests so it cannot be quietly abandoned.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Nehemiah shakes his lap and says so may the Most High shake out every man from his house and labor who does not perform this promise, and all the congregation says Amen and praises the Lord, and the people do according to the promise.
A visible sign seals the oath, and the whole congregation agrees, and the people keep the promise.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: From the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, twelve years as governor in Judah, Nehemiah and his brethren do not eat the bread of the governor.
Nehemiah refuses the provision owed to his office, governing for twelve years without taking from the people.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: The former governors were chargeable to the people, taking bread, wine, and forty shekels of silver, and their servants bore rule over the people, but Nehemiah does not do so because of the fear of God.
The fear of the Most High keeps Nehemiah from the burden and rule that earlier governors laid on the people.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Nehemiah continues in the work of the wall, buys no land, and gathers all his servants to the work.
He gives himself and his household to the labor rather than to gaining property.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Daily one ox, six choice sheep, and fowls are prepared for him, with store of wine every ten days, yet he does not require the bread of the governor because the bondage was heavy upon the people.
Though he provides a table, he refuses to charge the people for it, sparing them because their burden is already heavy.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Nehemiah asks the Most High to think upon him for good according to all he has done for the people.
Nehemiah was about the work and for the people, not the usery of the people, and he commits his labor to the remembrance of the Most High.

note.label: Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah Rebukes Usury Among the Brethren

points: Here is the bourgeoisie, the black bourgeoisie, in the scriptures. “And there was a great cry of the people and of their wives against their brethren the Jews.” They said they had to take up corn for these certain Jews that they might eat and live.

note.label: THE BLACK BOULÉ & BOURGEOISIE IN THE BIBLE

points: “We have mortgaged our lands, vineyards, and houses, that we might buy corn, because of the dearth.” “We have borrowed money for the king’s tribute”: we borrowed money to pay taxes.

note.label: THE BLACK BOULÉ & BOURGEOISIE IN THE BIBLE

points: “Lo, we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters are brought unto bondage already: neither is it in our power to redeem them.” Our sons and daughters are working for these other Jews, black Jews, and we can’t even redeem them, because we’re broke, “for other men have our lands and vineyards.”

note.label: THE BLACK BOULÉ & BOURGEOISIE IN THE BIBLE

points: Nehemiah was very angry, “and I rebuked the nobles, and the rulers.” The nobles were a group of intellectuals who were very wealthy. These are your bourgeois. “Ye exact usury, every one of his brother.” Usury means interest, extreme interest, like twenty percent.

note.label: THE BLACK BOULÉ & BOURGEOISIE IN THE BIBLE

points: “We after our ability have redeemed our brethren the Jews, which were sold unto the heathen; and will ye even sell your brethren?” See what we started to do to ourselves. We were redeemed from the Persians and Medes, we got back into our own land, and now we were putting each other in captivity. “Then held they their peace, and found nothing to answer.”

note.label: THE BLACK BOULÉ & BOURGEOISIE IN THE BIBLE

points: “It is not good that ye do.” “I pray you, let us leave off this usury”: leave off the interest you put on the people. “Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money”, the interest they took.

note.label: THE BLACK BOULÉ & BOURGEOISIE IN THE BIBLE

points: “We will restore them, and will require nothing of them.” “Then I called the priests, and took an oath of them.” Nehemiah got all Israel against the nobles. Sometimes a show of force is necessary to get these rich black people off your back, because at times they will do worse to you than the white man. That is what was going on in Nehemiah 5.

note.label: THE BLACK BOULÉ & BOURGEOISIE IN THE BIBLE

points: Now there was dissension among our own people. “And there was a great cry of the people and of their wives against their brethren the Jews.” Some said their sons and daughters were many and they needed corn to eat and live; some said “We have mortgaged our lands, vineyards, and houses, that we might buy corn, because of the dearth.” They mortgaged their houses and land because of the hard times. Others said “We have borrowed money for the king’s tribute”, to pay their taxes.

note.label: State of Decay

points: “Then I consulted with myself, and I rebuked the nobles, and the rulers, and said unto them, Ye exact usury, every one of his brother.” The nobles and rulers were in cahoots with the other nations and robbing the people, exacting usury that made them poor. It is the same today: we integrated, and now some of us in the Christian churches, the politicians, the Boule, exact usury and press our people to make us poorer.

“We after our ability have redeemed our brethren the Jews, which were sold unto the heathen; and will ye even sell your brethren?” We just redeemed them from the heathen and you want to sell them back? “Then held they their peace”: they had nothing to say, because they knew they were wrong.

note.label: State of Decay

points: “Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses”. He told the nobles to give it back, because it was all about us being together and having all things common.

note.label: State of Decay

points: This is the kind of leader Nehemiah was: “I and my brethren have not eaten the bread of the governor.” He did not exact usury like the nobles; he understood nation building.

“But the former governors that had been before me were chargeable unto the people”. That is why the people had waxed poor and mortgaged their lands to pay their taxes, the same as our people today. Nehemiah would keep it in house: “but so did not I, because of the fear of God.” He saw the decay of his people and went to build.

note.label: State of Decay
